text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

--- Danish insurer Codan sees new acquisition or merger possibilities in eastern Europe after it absorbed troubled insurance company Hafnia some years ago and following its cooperation with Norway's Fokus Bank.

--- An inquiry into why Denmark's largest bank, Den Danske Bank, granted huge credit to the North Atlantic Faroe Islands through its subsidiary, Foroya Banki, in the 1980s is coming under attack from politicians for hiding important facts, sparking calls for an explanation from Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen.

--- The Danish section of international environmental organisation Greenpeace lost more than 10 percent of its members in 1996 reducing members to 20,258, mainly due to a controversial action last summer against Danish industrial fishing in the North Sea, forcing it to consider staff cuts.

--- Denmark's defence will not be able to achieve targets of contributing 1,500 soldiers to participate in NATO peacekeeping forces in Bosnia this year. Denmark can only afford to send some 800 soldiers and defence staff organisations are urging politicians to grant more money for international forces in future.

--- Denmark's DSB Rail is to compete with telecom group Tele Danmark through cooperation with multinational telecom company Global One, jointly owned by U.S. Sprint, France Telecom and Deutsche Telekom. The accord goes into effect in a few weeks time with DSB aiming to become Denmark's second largest telecom firm within a few years.
--- The introduction of new mobile telephone systems in Denmark next year is expected to lead to a halving of prices.

--- 1996 could be the best year ever for Danish shareholders according to a new survey, with a total increase in Copenhagen stock value of 92 billion crowns, 10 percent of the increase attributable to pharmaceuticals group Novo Nordisk. The positive trend is seen continuing in 1997.
